text.title: Futures rebound 2%+ after AI rout; Nvidia bounces, CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler
text.summary: US stock futures point to a sharp bounce after Friday's rout. S&P 500 futures are up 2.5%, Nasdaq 100 futures 3.3%, Russell 2000 futures 2.2% and Dow futures 1.8%. The S&P 500 has fallen seven straight sessions, and the Nasdaq closed Friday 15.3% below its 1-month high. The bounce is concentrated in the battered AI and chip names, so it looks like relief rather than a resolution. Treasury yields fell sharply Friday, and the dollar is at a 1-month high. Gold is rebounding while oil keeps sliding. The VIX at 31.3 shows investors are still paying up for protection.
text.rates: The 10-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 4.91%, down 14 bp on the day and 24 bp over five days. That is five straight declines. The 2-year fell 13 bp to 4.63%. Falling yields are consistent with a flight to safety and growth worries. Lower yields would typically ease the discount-rate pressure on richly valued tech. The dollar index is up 0.2% to 104.04, a 1-month high, which can weigh on commodities and multinational earnings. Oil is lower and gold is rebounding.
text.breadth: Overseas sessions were mixed. Europe is higher, with the Euro Stoxx 50 up 0.8%, the DAX up 0.8% and the FTSE 100 up 0.6%, led by a partial chip rebound. Hong Kong's Hang Seng is little changed, down 0.1%. The latest Nikkei reading in the data, time-stamped Friday, shows a 5.1% drop, so Japan's current direction is unclear from this data. European gains and the futures bounce point to a stabilizing open, but the VIX near 31 signals nerves remain.
text.context: The S&P 500 is down 8.6% over five days and 10.9% from its 1-month high, with a seven-session losing streak. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap notes the S&P 500 was still up about 2.0% year to date as of Nov 20. Growth has been hit hardest, with the Russell 1000 Growth down 13.6% year to date against value up 18.9%. Technology fell 12.1% on the week, the worst sector, while consumer staples held up best.
text.takeaway: Sharp drawdowns and one-day rebounds are common in corrections, and they are a reminder of why diversification across sectors and styles matters. Value and defensive areas have held up better than growth this year, while the longer-term picture depends on earnings and rate trends, not any single day.
text.talk: Markets are rebounding this morning after a sharp AI-driven selloff last week, but volatility is still elevated. Tech has taken the brunt of it, while bonds and gold have offered some cushion.

drivers.t: Nasdaq 100 futures are up about 3% after a week in which AI worries kept hitting tech, even with Anthropic's record debut. Friday's cash session was severe: the Nasdaq fell 5.3% and the S&P 500 fell 3.7%. The FT notes that Nvidia and Sandisk are rising sharply pre-market. After a drop that size, dip-buying and short covering often produce outsized snapbacks in the most beaten-down names. Reuters cautions that jitters across the market are expected to continue.

MarketWatch reports Nvidia is rising after a weekend of developments, including the Trump administration pushing for Jensen Huang to be reinstated to lead the company. Nvidia is the AI trade's bellwether, so company-specific news moves the whole complex, from chips to data-center suppliers. A Reuters Market Talk piece says markets are still asking questions about Nvidia, data centers and the Fed. The headlines do not say how much of the rebound is tied to this news versus a general oversold bounce.

CrowdStrike will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at about $43.9 billion. MarketWatch notes cybersecurity stocks have been hot. A deal of this size shows corporate boards are still willing to commit capital despite the selloff. Bloomberg separately reports that Wall Street is heading toward a record year for M&A. Zscaler is among CNBC's biggest pre-market movers.

Bloomberg says the rout is reviving the question of a Fed 'put' under Warsh, with a December rate hike looming. NewEdge's Cameron Dawson says volatility may not be enough to make the Fed pause. She sees likely more pain before the correction ends, and a possible turn into a growth scare. If policy stays restrictive while equities fall, the risk is that tighter financial conditions feed back into growth. That tension helps explain why bonds rallied even as stocks sold off.

drivers.h: AI funding strain and chip contagion
drivers.t: Bloomberg reports the largest tech companies are getting more creative to borrow the hundreds of billions they want for AI investment. Heavy funding needs raise the bar for returns, which is part of why AI valuations are under scrutiny. The strain was global last week. European chip stocks fell more than 10%, then staged a partial rebound today. Today's gains in Europe suggest the selling was not confined to the US.

Gold is up about 2.9% to $3,617, after its sharpest weekly decline since March. It is still roughly 10% lower for the month. WTI crude is down 1.4% at $82.25 and about 20% lower over a month. WSJ notes oil extended losses despite persistent shipping attacks in the Persian Gulf, so geopolitical risk is not offsetting the demand and supply signals right now. Lower oil eases pressure on energy costs, which feed consumer inflation.
